title: One family emoji, three different "lengths": 1, 5, and 8
assumption: A string's length property tells you how many characters a person sees on screen.

input.display: "\u{1F468}\u200D\u{1F469}\u200D\u{1F467}" (man + ZWJ + woman + ZWJ + girl = one family emoji)
input.description: Any emoji picker's "family"/"couple with heart"/skin-tone-modified emoji, typed into a bio, nickname, or chat message with a character-count limit.

what_goes_wrong: The single glyph a user sees as ONE character reports length 8 in JavaScript's .length, 5 via JavaScript's [...s].length or Python's len(), and 1 via JavaScript's Intl.Segmenter grapheme count. A "max 10 characters" bio limit enforced with .length rejects two family emoji (16 code units) that the user sees as two characters, and truncating by any of the non-grapheme measures can cut the glyph apart (see the truncation exhibits).
why: JavaScript strings are sequences of UTF-16 code units, and .length counts those units; each of the three emoji here is outside the Basic Multilingual Plane, so it needs a surrogate pair (2 code units), giving 3×2 + 2 ZWJ = 8. Python strings are sequences of Unicode code points, and len() counts those; the same string is 3 emoji + 2 ZWJ = 5 code points (the spread operator [...s] in JavaScript iterates by code point too, also giving 5). But a person perceives the whole ZWJ-joined sequence as a single "grapheme cluster" — exactly one visual unit — which is what JavaScript's Intl.Segmenter({granularity: "grapheme"}) counts, and what Python's standard library has no built-in equivalent for.
fix: Enforce user-facing length limits with a grapheme-cluster counter, not raw .length/len(). In JavaScript use Intl.Segmenter (built in, no dependency); Python's standard library has no grapheme-cluster segmenter, so either accept code-point length as an approximation (it undercounts far less often than UTF-16 length) or add a UAX #29-compliant library.

sources.title: Unicode Standard Annex #29: Unicode Text Segmentation (grapheme clusters)
